video_title: I let the Internet Design A (Bad) Military - Orbital Strikes to Battleships, Arming Emutopia Special
gist: Perun runs a deliberately comedic procurement thought experiment - crowdsourced equipment picks (M7 rifle, T-14 Armata, Queen Elizabeth carriers, an aviation battleship, XL-UUV 'submarine carriers', orbital tungsten rods, space marines) for the fictional middle power Emutopia - and reverse-engineers plausible-sounding justifications for each. The serious payload is procurement economics: requirement wording rather than the tender determines the winner, individually defensible buys hollow out a force when summed, and opportunity cost plus creative reuse of existing platforms usually beats buying the shiny thing.

themes.theme: Requirement-Setting as the Real Selection Lever

insights.claim: Perun argues defence procurement outcomes are usually predetermined by how the initial requirement is written rather than by bias or corruption inside the evaluation process, since a single line item on dimensions, performance, armament, manufacturing arrangements or compatibility can decide the winner long before any individual design is assessed.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: To predict a defence tender's winner, read the requirements document rather than the shortlist - favoured suppliers are visible in the spec long before award.
insights.quote: I didn't have to specifically say, I want to rig the selection process in favor of the T-14 Armata. I just had to set much more reasonable-sounding parameters

insights.claim: Perun shows that 'risk reduction' clauses requiring a selected system to already be in service with a major military, or to have seen combat, are common-sense-sounding filters that in practice hand a competition to a predetermined incumbent regardless of the design's merit.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: In-service and combat-proven clauses are structural moats for established primes and a signal that a nominally open tender is not open.
insights.quote: This reduces Imutopia's risk because no major military would ever purchase a dud

insights.claim: Perun frames the central requirements-writing tension as being prescriptive enough to steer industry without writing out creative solutions or discovering late that the stated requirement was not the actual need, citing the B-2's 'wouldn't it be great' low-level bombing capability as costing multiple years of delay and engineering sacrifices.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: The requirement versus nice-to-have boundary is where schedule slip and cost growth are seeded - a practical screen for program risk.

insights.claim: Perun warns that individually defensible purchases become incoherent when summed, because tunnel vision on single platforms without a force-level concept leaves planners backward-engineering a strategy around capital ships they can no longer escort.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Assess national force plans at portfolio level - a plan that hollows the escort tier tends to force a corrective procurement cycle later.
insights.quote: It is entirely possible to put up a piece of equipment that by itself might come with a great sales pitch and an excellent stat sheet, and yet it not be the correct fit for the overall force.

insights.claim: Perun advocates a 'recycle before replace' logic check, arguing repurposing existing platforms is usually more efficient than wholesale replacement because replacement drags in a new sustainment plan and training program, and citing the Hawker Typhoon becoming a ground-attack aircraft and the Messerschmitt 110 becoming a night fighter.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Upgrade and role-change programs are a persistently underrated revenue pool relative to headline new-build platforms.
insights.quote: before you replace, it's decent to throw in a logic check to see if you can first recycle

insights.claim: Perun argues the decisive procurement and logistics consequence of shifting from 5.56 NATO to a higher-pressure round like the M7's is that larger rounds are larger, forcing soldiers either to significantly cut their ammunition load or spend more weight to carry the same round count.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Next-generation rifle programs carry a hidden logistics tax in magazine capacity, load carriage and resupply volume that never appears in the headline unit price.
insights.quote: it's that larger rounds are larger

insights.claim: Perun notes that abandoning 5.56 NATO forfeits ammunition cross-compatibility with a significant number of allied forces plus access to massive global stockpiles and production capacity - an interoperability and surge-supply cost that a national cartridge change quietly imposes.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Cartridge changes fragment the allied ammunition base and create long-tail demand for new production capacity instead of drawing on existing surplus.

insights.claim: Perun contends Ukraine's experience argues against heavier infantry rifles, because long dismounted movements make weight a premium and longer-range lethality against infantry there is delivered by FPV drones and artillery rather than small arms, so spare carrying capacity is better spent on drone batteries or a CQB shotgun.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: The demand signal favours infantry drone kit and load carriage over next-generation rifle programs - treat NGSW-style budgets as contestable.

themes.theme: Armour Economics and the High-Low Ground Mix

insights.claim: Perun highlights that Russia planned 2,300 T-14 Armatas by 2025 but built only a handful, with hesitation predating the Ukraine war - then-Deputy PM Yuri Borisov said in 2018 that money would go to upgraded older designs instead, claiming upgraded T-72s beat German, French and US MBTs on price, efficiency and quality with a budget ten times smaller than NATO's.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: A canonical case of a clean-sheet next-generation platform losing to upgrade economics - a structural tailwind for retrofit and modernisation contractors.
insights.quote: Why flood our military with Armatas? The T-72s are in great demand in the markets.

insights.claim: Perun demonstrates that a weight cap justified by bridges, airlift or landing craft, plus an uncrewed-turret requirement, minimum gun calibre, hard-kill active protection and a drone-swatting remote weapon station, is enough to eliminate the Leopard 2A8, a modernised Abrams and Challenger 3 while leaving the T-14 Armata technically compliant.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Weight limits and turret architecture clauses are the most powerful discriminators in MBT tenders and worth tracking in any live armour competition.

insights.claim: Perun notes demand for rugged civilian vehicles on the Ukrainian battlefield grew large enough that the Ukrainian MOD ran its own procurements for thousands of them to augment volunteer-supplied vehicles, with technicals used as guided-missile launch platforms and as anti-aircraft carriers in mobile fire groups downing Shahed-style drones.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Confirms a durable state-level procurement channel for commercial 4x4s and pickup conversions in high-intensity war, not just an improvised curiosity.

insights.claim: Perun argues mass corrugated-iron shelters - real shelters plus layered dummy shelters over aircraft, vehicles and stores - are an extremely cheap counter to satellite-based targeting because they impose a punishing cost exchange on an attacker's ballistic missile inventory.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Low-cost concealment and decoy infrastructure is an underpriced defensive investment relative to active missile defence.
insights.quote: they better be building billions in ballistic missiles to blow up a bunch of bulk buildings from Bunnings

insights.claim: Perun justifies buying roughly 100 Lamborghinis with only about 12 used for actual reconnaissance on the grounds that the real problem is recruitment and retention, arguing volunteer militaries must spend heavily on attracting and keeping personnel so a few cruise missiles' worth of spending on a recruiting hook can be rational.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Personnel attraction and retention is a real, growing and often unbudgeted competitor for hardware dollars in all-volunteer forces.
insights.quote: the problem we're trying to solve here isn't actually reconnaissance, it's recruitment and retention

themes.theme: Capital Ships and the Hollowed-Out Middle Fleet

insights.claim: Perun identifies three binding constraints on a middle power buying two Queen Elizabeth class carriers, each over 280 m and 80,000 tons: shipyards and workforce to build them on a reasonable timeline, costs that would cannibalise other critical naval investment unless stretched over an unreasonable period, and oppressive crew requirements.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Carrier ambitions for mid-tier navies are gated by yards and crews more than sticker price - watch drydock and workforce capacity as the binding constraint.

insights.claim: Perun floats a multinational 'time-share' carrier fleet across the UK, Canada and Emutopia - one procurement and maintenance plan for four hulls, deep maintenance in the UK, some servicing in the other two theatres - allowing one carrier permanently deployed and surge to two or three, at the cost of massive political complication over who gets the ships when.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Joint multinational capital-ship ownership would concentrate sustainment revenue in a single lead yard while breaking the one-nation-one-hull cost ceiling.

insights.claim: Perun exposes the standard multi-role funding trick: a Swiss Army knife combatant is affordable only by cutting the specialised LHA/LHD, frigate, destroyer, hospital ship and command ship that each did the job better, and concentrating those capabilities in one hull removes the option of having them in several places at once.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Multi-mission consolidation pitches should be stress-tested against dispersion value - the offsets funding them usually destroy fleet flexibility.

insights.claim: Perun characterises the resulting fleet as top and bottom-heavy, with displacement and manpower concentrated in carriers and battleships and the remainder in underwater drones, leaving minesweepers, patrol boats, corvettes, frigates and destroyers short-funded while every remaining escort is tied to carrier protection.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Escort and mine-warfare shortfalls are the predictable second-order consequence of capital-ship-led naval plans and a recurring source of later emergency procurement.

insights.claim: Perun proposes turning extra-large UUVs such as Australia's Ghost Shark and America's Orca into drone carriers via a payload module launching FPVs or loitering munitions, arguing it is an incremental ask because navies already treat XL-UUVs as multi-purpose payload carriers for sensors, robotic payloads and mines at comparatively low cost versus crewed submarines.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Payload-module ecosystems rather than the hulls are where XL-UUV value accrues - watch modular payload contracts around Ghost Shark and Orca.

insights.claim: Perun notes Ukraine has repeatedly launched FPVs from small surface drones, trading warhead size for reusability, range and precision, and used them against soft, valuable, hard-to-conceal coastal targets like radars and air defence installations that must sit in specific places and are very fragile.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: The drone-carrying-drone pattern is battle-proven and is the template for the next generation of uncrewed maritime strike.

insights.claim: Perun argues uncrewed submarines are far easier to surge in wartime than crewed ones because trained and experienced crews cannot be rush-built, so designing XL-UUVs for mass production - tooling in advance, stockpiled long-lead items, maximum commercial off-the-shelf content - lets a state 'hit print' on a navy given warning of a crisis.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Warm tooling and long-lead-item stockpiling is the concrete fundable form of mobilisation readiness, a spending category distinct from platform buys.

insights.claim: Perun frames a drone-heavy navy as explicitly optimised for deterrence by punishment rather than denial, applying lessons from Ukraine, Iran and the Houthis with better technology and more scale to make opposing ports prohibitively risky for civilian traffic and pin down disproportionate anti-submarine warfare assets - while conceding there is only so much disaster relief you can do with a robotic submarine.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Punishment-based maritime deterrence favours cheap distributed effectors and mines over blue-water escorts, but sacrifices the peacetime presence roles that dominate political tasking.
insights.quote: We don't try and go down the road of deterrence by denial. We don't have the resources for it. Instead, the name of the game is deterrence by punishment.

insights.claim: Perun relays RAND's 2002 'Space Weapons Earth Wars' constraint that long, slender, heavy, non-explosive orbital penetrators are useful only against targets vulnerable to vertical penetration - tall buildings, missile silos, ships and hardened aircraft shelters - and not against runways, deeply buried bunkers, bridges or low, long buildings.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Rod-from-God target sets are far narrower than popular perception, which caps the achievable military value of any such program.
insights.quote: Suitable weapons would include tall buildings, missile silos, ships, and hardened aircraft shelters, but not runways, deeply buried bunkers, bridges, and low, long buildings.

insights.claim: Perun cites RAND's sizing example of a roughly 1 m, 100 kg rod penetrating about 1.5 m of steel, versus other studies contemplating 100-plus-ton rods, and notes global responsive coverage implies an absentee ratio of roughly six satellites for every one usefully on station.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: The absentee ratio is the hidden multiplier that makes orbital strike constellations economically brutal, and the same logic applies to any responsive-coverage space architecture.
insights.quote: Space-based kinetic energy weapons directed at surface targets are very difficult to defend against because of their very high velocity and very brief flight through the atmosphere.

insights.claim: Perun argues orbital kinetic strike is dominated on cost by terrestrial alternatives in 2026 - hard-to-intercept ballistic missiles such as Russia's RS-24 and China's DF-21 plus hypersonic glide vehicles like the DF-17 and America's Dark Eagle - so the only way to justify the space option is to write a genuinely global deny-sanctuary requirement that long range alone cannot satisfy.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Expanding hypersonic and ballistic inventories keep crowding out orbital strike on cost per effect - a reason to discount space-strike program hype.

insights.claim: Perun identifies collapsing launch costs as the one variable that genuinely improved the orbital strike case since 2003, citing a recent US contract for another 18 Falcon 9 launches over 14 months at about 1.6 billion US dollars, while cautioning those figures do not transfer to lifting classified or oversized payloads.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Commercial launch pricing is the key input that makes previously absurd space architectures financially arguable - a structural tailwind for launch providers.

insights.claim: Perun argues an orbital rod system's real return may be psychological rather than military, noting many weapons across history commanded more public fear than their raw capabilities merited, so marginal spend might be better placed on media presence than on more satellites and rods - while conceding the system would be massively vulnerable to anti-satellite launchers and would push its owner toward first-strike postures.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Perceived capability can substitute for real capability in deterrence, so headline weapons announcements often read as signalling rather than capability.
insights.quote: you can name plenty of weapon systems across history that have commanded more public attention, more fear, and more apprehension than their actual raw capabilities merited

themes.theme: Dual-Use Space Programs and Cheap Resilience

insights.claim: Perun quantifies lunar base ambition as out of reach for an individual middle power by noting NASA's plan calls for more than 80 launches to the moon and delivery of north of 210 tons of cargo, a scale no single mid-tier nation can realistically match.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Lunar infrastructure economics force coalition or commercial participation - single-nation lunar programs are not credible at that cargo scale.

insights.claim: Perun's general lesson for well-funded pet projects is to technically deliver exactly what you were told to do while generating as many genuinely useful outcomes as possible on the side, illustrated by building astronaut selection and training, sovereign launch and landing, rovers and habitats under cover of a 'space marine' mandate.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Dual-use structuring is how exotic political mandates get converted into durable industrial capability, and a lens for reading seemingly absurd defence line items.
insights.quote: You find a way to technically deliver exactly what you're being told to do while on the side making sure you generate as many actually useful outcomes as possible.

insights.claim: Perun argues the hard part of a military space program is space itself rather than the weapons, noting Cold War studies of lunar infantry combat envisaged very light, simple small arms and the Soviet Almaz space gun was relatively simple, so a weapons mandate can fund expensive general-purpose capability and be dropped cheaply when political priorities change.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Military space budgets reliably subsidise civilian-usable launch, habitat and crew capability - the classic R&D spillover pattern, now applied to lunar programs.
insights.quote: it's not so much that weaponizing space is hard, it's just that space is hard

insights.claim: Perun endorses cheap resilience measures suited to an EW-saturated battlefield where signature management matters, specifically burying power and fibre optic cable to prepared defensive positions in a pre-war period to sustain infantry and guarantee connectivity for forward UAS and UGVs, plus balloons and zeppelins as cheap airborne sensor and drone-relay platforms.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Fibre, buried power and cheap high-altitude platforms are low-cost, high-leverage counter-EW investments already validated in Ukraine.

insights.claim: Perun's honest verdict is that the crowdsourced Emutopian package would be a bad investment and that outsourcing a major procurement to the internet is inadvisable, while noting many submissions received outside Patreon were serious alternative force designs rather than attempts to sabotage the brief.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Frames the episode as a deliberate thought experiment - the specific buys are illustrative, while the requirements-writing and opportunity-cost lessons are the transferable content.
insights.quote: Would it be a good investment? No, but it would be an investment.
